claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in more than 293.0 million infections and more than 5.46 million deaths as of January 4, 2022.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic, starting in the last months of 2019 in Wuhan (China) and caused by the RNA virus SARS-CoV-2, so far (January 4, 2022) has resulted in more than 293.0 million (Mio) infections and more than 5.46 Mio deaths (data source: https://www.worldometers.info/coronavirus/).
evidence: The claim cites a specific data source (worldometers.info) for the infection and death statistics.

claim: Four COVID-19 vaccines have received conditional market authorizations by regulatory bodies: BioNTech/Pfizer (BTN162b2/Comirnaty), Moderna (mRNA-1273/Spikevax), AstraZeneca (AZD1222/ChAdOx1-S/Vaxzevria), and Janssen (Ad26.COV2.S).
source: The world has faced the fastest development and production of vaccines ever, resulting in a total of four vaccines that have received conditional market authorizations by the regulatory bodies: the mRNA vaccines from BioNTech/Pfizer (BTN162b2/Comirnaty; EMA: 21.12.20) and Moderna (mRNA-1273/Spikevax; EMA: 6.1.21), as well as the adenoviral vector-based vaccines from AstraZeneca (AZD1222/ChAdOx1-S/Vaxzevria; EMA: 29.1.21) and Janssen (Ad26.COV2.S; EMA: 11.3.21).
evidence: The claim provides specific vaccine names, manufacturers, and EMA authorization dates.

claim: All four COVID-19 vaccines encode slightly different forms of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein.
source: All four vaccines encode slightly different forms of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein, which mediates virus binding to the host cell membrane and entry via ACE2 and TMPRSS2, respectively (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2020 regarding Spike protein function.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein mediates virus binding to the host cell membrane and entry via ACE2 and TMPRSS2.
source: All four vaccines encode slightly different forms of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein, which mediates virus binding to the host cell membrane and entry via ACE2 and TMPRSS2, respectively (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2020.

claim: Severe side effects including thromboses (ITP) or thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome (TTS) were first observed with Vaxzevria in Europe in March 2021.
source: While vaccination with BioNTech and Moderna mostly causes only mild and typical immediate vaccination side effects, severe side effects thromboses (ITP) or thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome (TTS) were first observed with Vaxzevria in Europe (in March 2021).
evidence: The claim provides a specific timeframe and vaccine name for the observation of severe side effects.

claim: The most severe side effects of Vaxzevria entailed rare events of thrombocytopenia combined with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).
source: The most severe side effects entailed rare events of thrombocytopenia combined with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).
evidence: The claim describes specific clinical manifestations observed with the vaccine.

claim: The higher than expected occurrence of CVST led to a rapid suspension of the Vaxzevria vaccination campaign in several European countries in March 2021.
source: The higher than expected occurrence of CVST led to a rapid suspension of the Vaxzevria vaccination campaign in several European countries (March 11–14, 2021: Denmark, several northern European countries, Thailand, Ireland; March 15, 2021: Germany, Italy, France, and Spain).
evidence: The claim provides specific dates and countries where vaccination campaigns were suspended.

claim: According to the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute in Germany (report dated December 23, 2021), thrombocytopenia and immunothrombocytopenia (ITP) have been observed in 314 cases after 96.6 million vaccination doses with Comirnaty (3.3 cases per million injections).
source: Thrombocytopenia and immunothrombocytopenia (ITP) have been observed in 314 cases after 96.6 Mio vaccination doses with Comirnaty (3.3 cases per Mio injections)
evidence: The claim cites specific data from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report and is also shown in Table 1.

claim: According to the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute in Germany (report dated December 23, 2021), thrombocytopenia and immunothrombocytopenia (ITP) have been observed in 28 cases after 10.5 million vaccination doses with Spikevax (2.6 cases per million injections).
source: in 28 cases with Spikevax after 10.5 Mio vaccination doses with Comirnaty (2.6 cases per Mio injections)
evidence: The claim cites specific data from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report and is also shown in Table 1.

claim: According to the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute in Germany (report dated December 23, 2021), thrombocytopenia and immunothrombocytopenia (ITP) have been observed in 269 cases after 12.7 million vaccination doses with Vaxzevria (21.2 cases per million injections).
source: in 269 with Vaxzevria after 12.7 Mio vaccination doses cases (21.2 cases per Mio injections)
evidence: The claim cites specific data from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report and is also shown in Table 1.

claim: According to the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute in Germany (report dated December 23, 2021), thrombocytopenia and immunothrombocytopenia (ITP) have been observed in 23 cases after 3.4 million vaccination doses with Ad26.COV2.S (6.6 cases per million injections).
source: and in 23 cases with Ad26.COV2.S after 3.4 Mio vaccination doses cases (6.6 cases per Mio injections).
evidence: The claim cites specific data from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report and is also shown in Table 1.

claim: Thrombosis-related death cases for Comirnaty, Spikevax, Vaxzevria, and Ad26.COV2.S were 74, 6, 81, and 12, respectively.
source: Thrombosis-related death cases for these four vaccines were 74, 6, 81, and 12, respectively.
evidence: The claim provides specific death case numbers from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report, also shown in Table 1.

claim: Thromboembolic events associated with case mortality were in the range of 21.4–52%.
source: This indicates that thromboembolic events associated with case mortality were in the range of 21.4–52% (see Table 1).
evidence: The claim provides a calculated range based on data presented in Table 1.

claim: TTS has been observed in 36, 5, 200, and 24 patients for Comirnaty, Spikevax, Vaxzevria, and Ad26.COV2.S, respectively, indicating a relative risk of 0.4, 0.5, 15.7, and 6.9 cases per million injections.
source: TTS has been observed for these four vaccines in 36, 5, 200, and 24 patients, indicating a relative risk of 0.4, 0.5, 15.7, and 6.9 cases per Mio injections.
evidence: The claim cites specific TTS case numbers and calculated risks from the Paul-Ehrlich-Institute report, also shown in Table 1.

claim: Thromboembolic events in combination with thrombocytopenia share similarities with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
source: These thromboembolic events in combination with thrombocytopenia share similarities with another condition, 'heparin-induced thrombocytopenia' (HIT).
evidence: The claim draws a comparison between vaccine-induced events and a known medical condition.

claim: The term 'vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia' (VITT) was coined for the vaccine-induced condition after finding that autoantibodies against the platelet factor 4 (PF4) could be causally linked to it.
source: The term 'vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia' (VITT) was coined for this vaccine-induced condition, after finding out that autoantibodies against the platelet factor 4 (PF4) could be causally linked to it (Greinacher et al., 2021b; Greinacher et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Greinacher et al., 2021a and 2021b regarding the mechanism of VITT.

claim: Despite intensive research activities by many laboratories, the underlying initiating mechanisms for the observed side events were not yet fully understood.
source: However, despite intensive research activities by many laboratories, the underlying initiating mechanisms for the observed side events were not yet fully understood.
evidence: The claim acknowledges gaps in scientific understanding at the time of writing.

claim: mRNA vaccines encode the Spike sequence as a modified RNA sequence encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles.
source: The mRNA vaccines encode, as the naming implies, the Spike sequence as a modified RNA sequence encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles.
evidence: The claim describes the basic structure of mRNA vaccines.

claim: Upon intramuscular injection of mRNA vaccines, the nanoparticles are taken up by cells, where the mRNA cargo is released into the cytosol.
source: Upon intramuscular injection, the nanoparticles are taken up by the cells, where the mRNA cargo is released into the cytosol.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of mRNA vaccine delivery.

claim: Both mRNA vaccines encode a signal peptide, so the process of protein translation occurs at the rough endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) and results in membrane-anchored Spike proteins.
source: Since both mRNA vaccines encode a signal peptide, the process of protein translation occurs at the rough endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) and results in membrane-anchored Spike proteins.
evidence: The claim describes the cellular processing of mRNA vaccine-encoded proteins.

claim: Further post-translational modifications of Spike protein occur in the ER and Golgi apparatus (glycosylation) from where the Spike protein trimer is transported in vesicles to the outer cell membrane.
source: Further post-translational modifications occur in the ER and Golgi apparatus (glycosylation) from where the Spike protein trimer is transported in vesicles to the outer cell membrane.
evidence: The claim describes the cellular processing pathway for Spike protein.

claim: Adenoviral vector-based vaccines deliver the Spike sequence as a codon-optimized DNA sequence instead of a RNA sequence.
source: In contrast, adenoviral vector-based vaccines deliver the Spike sequence as a codon-optimized DNA sequence instead of a RNA sequence.
evidence: The claim describes the fundamental difference between adenoviral and mRNA vaccines.

claim: Vaxzevria is based on a genetically modified chimpanzee adenovirus type Y25, which is replication incompetent.
source: Vaxzevria is based on a genetically modified chimpanzee adenovirus type Y25, while the Janssen vaccine is based on a human adenovirus type 26 (HAdV-D26), both of which are replication incompetent.
evidence: The claim describes the viral vector used in the Vaxzevria vaccine.

claim: The Janssen vaccine is based on a human adenovirus type 26 (HAdV-D26), which is replication incompetent.
source: Vaxzevria is based on a genetically modified chimpanzee adenovirus type Y25, while the Janssen vaccine is based on a human adenovirus type 26 (HAdV-D26), both of which are replication incompetent.
evidence: The claim describes the viral vector used in the Janssen vaccine.

claim: Upon transduction of the host cell and disassembly of the adenoviral vector particle, the linear double-stranded DNA is released and enters the nucleus.
source: Upon transduction of the host cell and disassembly of the vector particle, the linear double-stranded DNA is released and enters the nucleus.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of adenoviral vector transduction.

claim: Viral DNA-encoded genes become transcribed using the host cell transcription machinery after adenoviral DNA enters the nucleus.
source: Subsequently, viral DNA-encoded genes become transcribed using the host cell transcription machinery (Doerfler and Böhm, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Doerfler and Böhm, 2003.

claim: In the nucleus and before the mRNA is exported to the cytosol for translation, the resulting RNA molecule from adenoviral vectors is subject to the same post-transcriptional RNA processing machinery as endogenous primary transcripts, including the possibility of splicing.
source: In the nucleus and before the mRNA is exported to the cytosol for translation (see above), the resulting RNA molecule is subject to the same post-transcriptional RNA processing machinery as endogenous primary transcripts, including the possibility of splicing.
evidence: The claim describes the nuclear processing of adenoviral vector-derived transcripts.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is a single-stranded RNA virus of the betacoronavirus family that naturally has a purely cytoplasmic replication cycle.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is a single-stranded RNA virus of the betacoronavirus family that naturally has a purely cytoplasmic replication cycle.
evidence: The claim describes the basic biology of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Coronaviruses have not been exposed to any evolutionary pressure that would have an impact on biological processes taking place in the nucleus.
source: Therefore, coronaviruses have not been exposed to any evolutionary pressure that would have an impact on biological processes taking place in the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cytoplasmic replication cycle of coronaviruses.

claim: Almost all nuclear-encoded genes contain introns that become eliminated from precursor RNA transcripts by the splice machinery.
source: Almost all nuclear-encoded genes contain introns that become eliminated from precursor RNA transcripts by the splice machinery (Lee and Rio, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee and Rio, 2015.

claim: Defined RNA consensus sequences are recognized by RNA/protein complexes (spliceosome), which consist of nearly 100 proteins and specific U-RNAs.
source: Defined RNA consensus sequences are recognized by RNA/protein complexes (spliceosome), which consist of nearly 100 proteins and specific U-RNAs.
evidence: The claim describes the composition of the spliceosome.

claim: Splice events are influenced by exonic splice enhancer sequences and exonic splice silencer sequences, which bind splice-activating or -suppressing proteins.
source: Noteworthy, splice events are influenced by exonic splice enhancer sequences and exonic splice silencer sequences, which bind splice-activating or -suppressing proteins.
evidence: The claim describes regulatory mechanisms of splicing.

claim: During the splice process, a 'branch A' nucleotide performs a nucleophilic attack at a G•G-dinucleotide of the 5'-splice consensus sequence G•GUNNGU.
source: During this evolutionary conserved splice process, a so-called 'branch A' nucleotide is performing a nucleophilic attack at a G•G-dinucleotide of the 5'-splice consensus sequence G•GUNNGU.
evidence: The claim describes the molecular mechanism of splicing.

claim: The resulting 3'-OH of the final exonic G nucleotide makes a second nucleophilic attack at the G•G-dinucleotide of the 3'-splice consensus sequence YYYYYCAG•G.
source: The resulting 3'-OH of the final exonic G nucleotide then makes a second nucleophilic attack at the G•G-dinucleotide of the 3'-splice consensus sequence YYYYYCAG•G.
evidence: The claim describes the molecular mechanism of splicing.

claim: During splicing, two exons become fused, and the intronic sequence is eliminated.
source: To this end, two exons become fused, and the intronic sequence is being eliminated.
evidence: The claim describes the outcome of the splicing process.

claim: When using cloned cDNA in molecular biology or biotechnology, no intronic sequences are usually present, because cDNA synthesis is made from already spliced mRNA molecules.
source: When using cloned cDNA in molecular biology or biotechnology, no intronic sequences are usually present, because cDNA synthesis is made from already spliced mRNA molecules.
evidence: The claim describes standard molecular biology practice.

claim: In the case of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the cloned cDNA for the Spike open reading frame was not coming from a nuclear-encoded gene, but from an RNA virus that replicates solely in the cytosol of infected cells.
source: However, in case of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the cloned cDNA for the Spike open reading frame was not coming from a nuclear-encoded gene, rather from an RNA virus that replicates solely in the cytosol of infected cells.
evidence: The claim describes the origin of the Spike cDNA used in vaccines.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike cDNA exhibits potential SD and SA sites just by chance (~130 cryptic splice signal sequences in the total SARS-CoV-2 virus sequence), because no negative selection has ever taken place during the evolution of coronavirus to eliminate such sequences.
source: Therefore, such a cDNA exhibits potential SD and SA sites just by chance (~130 cryptic splice signal sequences in the total SARS-CoV-2 virus sequence), because no negative selection has ever taken place during the evolution of coronavirus to eliminate such sequences.
evidence: The claim provides a specific number of cryptic splice sites and explains their presence through evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Nuclear splicing of DNA-encoded Spike RNA sequences might result in spliced, and thus, truncated Spike protein variants with unknown fate and function.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that nuclear splicing of DNA-encoded Spike RNA sequences might result in spliced, and thus, truncated Spike protein variants with unknown fate and function.
evidence: The claim presents the authors' hypothesis.

claim: Cryptic splicing occurs only if strong splice sites are present, and thus, these cryptic splice sites will be used equally in different cell types or tissues.
source: Cryptic splicing occurs only if strong splice sites are present, and thus, these cryptic splice sites will be used equally in different cell types or tissues.
evidence: The claim describes the nature of cryptic splicing.

claim: The wildtype Spike open reading frame of the Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 isolate contains six splice donor (SD) sites and five splice acceptor (SA) sites with scores >0.15 as predicted by SpliceRover.
source: Therefore, we decided to filter these hits by their individual scores to identify those, which were used with a higher likelihood (wildtype Spike gene: six splice donor [SD] sites, five splice acceptor [SA] sites, see Figure 1 and Table 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis using SpliceRover and is shown in Figure 1 and Table 2A.

claim: Codon optimization resulted in an increased number of potential splice sites in all three adenoviral-encoded Spike sequences compared to the wildtype Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 Spike sequence.
source: Analyses revealed that codon optimization resulted in an increased number of potential splice sites in all three adenoviral-encoded Spike sequences (Ad5.S: 12 SD sites, 10 SA sites; ChAdOx1-S: 13 SD and 5 SA sites, Ad26.COV2.S: 9 SD and 10 SA sites, see Table 2B–D) compared to the open reading frame of the wildtype Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 Spike sequence.
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis and is shown in Table 2B-D.

claim: The Ad5.S codon-optimized Spike sequence contains 12 SD sites and 10 SA sites as predicted by SpliceRover.
source: Analyses revealed that codon optimization resulted in an increased number of potential splice sites in all three adenoviral-encoded Spike sequences (Ad5.S: 12 SD sites, 10 SA sites; ChAdOx1-S: 13 SD and 5 SA sites, Ad26.COV2.S: 9 SD and 10 SA sites, see Table 2B–D) compared to the open reading frame of the wildtype Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 Spike sequence.
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis and is shown in Table 2B.

claim: The ChAdOx1-S codon-optimized Spike sequence contains 13 SD sites and 5 SA sites as predicted by SpliceRover.
source: Analyses revealed that codon optimization resulted in an increased number of potential splice sites in all three adenoviral-encoded Spike sequences (Ad5.S: 12 SD sites, 10 SA sites; ChAdOx1-S: 13 SD and 5 SA sites, Ad26.COV2.S: 9 SD and 10 SA sites, see Table 2B–D) compared to the open reading frame of the wildtype Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 Spike sequence.
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis and is shown in Table 2C.

claim: The Ad26.COV2.S codon-optimized Spike sequence contains 9 SD sites and 10 SA sites as predicted by SpliceRover.
source: Analyses revealed that codon optimization resulted in an increased number of potential splice sites in all three adenoviral-encoded Spike sequences (Ad5.S: 12 SD sites, 10 SA sites; ChAdOx1-S: 13 SD and 5 SA sites, Ad26.COV2.S: 9 SD and 10 SA sites, see Table 2B–D) compared to the open reading frame of the wildtype Wuhan SARS-CoV-2 Spike sequence.
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis and is shown in Table 2D.

claim: In the wildtype Spike splice trap system, the '+2 construct' exhibited the strongest intracellular Luciferase activity (1291 relative light units).
source: Analyses of all three splice trap constructs in Luciferase assay revealed that the '+2 construct' exhibited the strongest intracellular Luciferase activity (1291 relative light units), while the '0 construct' resulted in a much lower activity (341 relative light units).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the wildtype Spike splice trap system, the '0 construct' resulted in a much lower Luciferase activity (341 relative light units).
source: Analyses of all three splice trap constructs in Luciferase assay revealed that the '+2 construct' exhibited the strongest intracellular Luciferase activity (1291 relative light units), while the '0 construct' resulted in a much lower activity (341 relative light units).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Small amounts of Luciferase activity were present extracellularly in the medium of cultured cells with wildtype Spike splice trap constructs, and this amount increased over time.
source: We also analyzed the medium of the cultured cells and observed that small amounts of Luciferase activity were present also extracellularly. This amount increased over time and mimicked relative ratios of the three constructs observed intracellularly (see Figure 2, panels II, III).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Due to the design of the splice traps, Luciferase activity can only be detected when splicing occurs.
source: Due to the design of the three splice traps, Luciferase activity can only be detected when splicing occurs.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design of the splice trap system.

claim: If splicing occurs between an SD in the Spike open reading frame and the SA in the splice trap, the C-terminally located TM domain of the Spike protein serving as the membrane anchor will get lost.
source: If splicing occurs between an SD in the Spike open reading frame and the SA in the splice trap, the C-terminally located TM domain of the Spike protein serving as the membrane anchor will get lost.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the splice trap design.

claim: Truncated Spike proteins lacking the TM domain may become secreted.
source: Thus, resulting truncated Spike proteins may become secreted.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of the membrane anchor.

claim: All three codon-optimized Spike genes derived from the different adenoviral vectors displayed a strong production of Spike-Luciferase fusion proteins that was enhanced compared to wildtype Spike sequence constructs.
source: All three codon-optimized Spike genes derived from the different adenoviral vectors displayed a strong production of Spike-Luciferase fusion proteins that was also enhanced compared to wildtype Spike sequence constructs.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The highest Luciferase activity of 15,840 relative light units was detected with the reading frame +1 of the ChAdOx1-S construct.
source: The highest activity of 15,840 relative light units was detected with the reading frame +1 of the ChAdOx1-S construct.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The lowest level of Luciferase activity among codon-optimized constructs was found in the Ad26.COV2.S construct.
source: The lowest level of Luciferase activity was found in the Ad26.COV2.S construct.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Western blot analysis detected strong signals of proteins with sizes of 95–250 kDa in cell lysates with both anti-Spike and anti-Luciferase antibodies, confirming Spike-Luciferase fusion proteins of different lengths.
source: As shown in Figure 3, for all analyzed Spike splice traps strong signals of proteins with sizes of 95–250 kDa were detected in cell lysates with both antibodies, confirming Spike-Luciferase fusion proteins of different lengths.
evidence: The claim is based on Western blot experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cell lysate and medium supernatant of each investigated cell line displayed several protein bands migrating at molecular weights as predicted by the major splice events.
source: Cell lysate and medium supernatant of each investigated cell line displayed several protein bands migrating at molecular weights as predicted by the major splice events in each of the investigated cell lines (Ad5.S 195.1 and 195.3 kDa; ChAdOX1-S 195.1 and 195.3 kDa; Ad26.COV2.S 196.4 kDa; all without glycosylation).
evidence: The claim is based on Western blot experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Several splice reactions from predicted splice sites (e.g. SD1-3) were observed in wildtype Spike-encoding splice trap constructs by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing.
source: As shown in Figure 4, we observed several splice reactions from predicted splice sites (e.g. SD1-3), but also internal splice reactions that lead to frame-shift events.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two splice events downstream of the ACE2-binding domain were found resulting in a fusion between Spike and Luciferase.
source: We also found two splice events downstream of the ACE2-binding domain resulting again in a fusion between Spike and Luciferase.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 5'-non-coding sequence of the pIX transcription unit of the three different adenovirus types contains a highly conserved SA site behind the pIX promoter and upstream of the pIX ATG start codon.
source: The 5'-non-coding sequence of the pIX transcription unit of the three different adenovirus types contains a highly conserved SA site behind the pIX promoter and upstream of the pIX ATG start codon (Ad5.S pIX at nucleotide –14; ChAdOx1-S pIX at nucleotide –4; Ad26.COV2.S pIX at nucleotide –5).
evidence: The claim provides specific nucleotide positions for the SA sites in each vector.

claim: All three Spike genes of the different adenoviral vector backbones displayed splice events to the adenoviral pIX transcript.
source: As shown in Figures 5 and 6, Figure 7 all three Spike genes of the different adenoviral vector backbones displayed splice events to the adenoviral pIX transcript.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Although all Spike genes contain a poly(A) signal sequence that should initiate the poly-adenylation process, transcriptional read-through allowing the detected splice events to occur was observed in all cases.
source: Noteworthy, although all Spike genes contain a poly(A) signal sequence that should initiate the poly-adenylation process, in all cases we observed transcriptional read-through allowing the detected splice events to occur.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR data showing read-through transcripts.

claim: The Ad5.S Spike gene displayed predominant splice events at positions 506, 1821, 3610*, 3,614, and 3641* to the SA within the pIX transcript.
source: The Ad5.S Spike gene displayed the predominant splice events at positions 506, 1821, 3610*, 3,614, and 3641* to the SA within the pIX transcript of the vector backbone (numbers with an asterisk were not predicted by SpliceRover).
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ChAdOx1-S Spike gene displayed predominant splice events at positions 506, 1049*, 1914*, 3610*, 3614 and –298* and –84*.
source: The ChAdOx1-S Spike gene displayed the predominant splice events at positions 506, 1049*, 1914*, 3610*, 3614 and –298* and –84*.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Two splice events in ChAdOx1-S involved an SD located in the bovine growth hormone (BGH) poly(A) signal 298 and 84 nucleotides upstream of the pIX start codon.
source: The latter two splice events involved an SD located in the bovine growth hormone (BGH) poly(A) signal 298 and 84 nucleotides upstream of the pIX start codon.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The Ad26.COV2.S Spike gene displayed weak splice events occurring at nucleotide 541*, 959*, 1184, 1221*, 3641*, and –83*.
source: Finally, the Ad26.COV2.S Spike gene displayed weak splice events occurring at nucleotide 541*, 959*, 1184, 1221*, 3641*, and –83*.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: One splice event in Ad26.COV2.S involved an SD in the simian virus 40 (SV40) poly(A) signal sequence located –83 nucleotides upstream of the pIX start codon.
source: Also here one splice event involved an SD in the simian virus 40 (SV40) poly(A) signal sequence located –83 nucleotides upstream of the pIX start codon.
evidence: The claim is based on RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PCR amplification of Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-transduced HeLa cells samples showed additional DNA bands of shorter lengths, confirming splicing at different positions within the read-through sequences.
source: While in Ad26.COV2.S-transduced HeLa cells no truncated cDNA fragments were detected, PCR amplification of Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-transduced HeLa cells samples showed additional DNA bands of shorter lengths, confirming splicing at different positions within the read-through sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: In Ad26.COV2.S-transduced HeLa cells no truncated cDNA fragments were detected.
source: While in Ad26.COV2.S-transduced HeLa cells no truncated cDNA fragments were detected, PCR amplification of Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-transduced HeLa cells samples showed additional DNA bands of shorter lengths, confirming splicing at different positions within the read-through sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sequencing of the shortest DNA fragment of Ad5.S-transduced samples revealed that splicing occurred in-frame from the predicted SD site upstream of the TM domain of the Spike protein to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon, resulting in a potentially secreted fusion protein.
source: Interestingly, sequencing of the shortest DNA fragment of Ad5.S-transduced samples (Figure 9, red arrow) revealed that splicing occurred in-frame from the predicted SD site upstream of the TM domain of the Spike protein to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon (Figure 5, splice site at nt 3610), resulting in a potentially secreted fusion protein.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sequencing of the shortest DNA fragment of ChAdOx1-S-transduced samples revealed splicing between the predicted SD site upstream of the TM of the Spike protein to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon, resulting in the generation of a stop codon.
source: Similar results were obtained from sequencing of the shortest DNA fragment of ChAdOx1-S-transduced samples (Figure 9A: blue arrow): splicing took place between the predicted SD site upstream of the TM of the Spike protein (Figure 6, splice site at nt 3610) to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon (Figure 9F). However, this splicing event resulted in the generation of a stop codon, thus no fusion but though secreted, truncated proteins would be translated due to the lacking TM domain.
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sequencing of the most abundant DNA fragment in ChAdOx1-S samples revealed splicing from the predicted SD site within the BGH poly(A) tail to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon.
source: Sequencing of the most abundant DNA fragment in ChAdOx1-S samples (Figure 9, white arrow) revealed splicing from the predicted SD site within the BGH poly(A) tail to the SA site upstream of the pIX start codon (Figure 6, splice site at nt –298).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The total amount of PCR-generated DNA indicates significant higher Spike-pIX read-through copy numbers for Ad5.S-transduced HeLa samples than ChAdOx1-S-transduced HeLa samples.
source: Comparing the total amount of PCR-generated DNA indicates significant higher Spike-pIX read-through copy numbers (and subsequent potential splicing) for Ad5.S-transduced HeLa samples than ChAdOx1-S-transduced HeLa samples (note even 2.5-fold less volume of PCR samples was loaded for Ad5.S; Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The BGH poly(A) of ChAdOx1-S is more potent than the SV40 poly(A) of Ad5.S to prevent read-through transcription into the pIX gene.
source: Since expression cassettes of both vectors are under the control of the identical hCMV promoter, this data suggests that the BGH poly(A) of ChAdOx1-S is more potent than the SV40 poly(A) of Ad5.S to prevent read-through transcription into the pIX gene.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the PCR data comparing Ad5.S and ChAdOx1-S.

claim: The abundance of splicing events has been cell type-dependent.
source: Interestingly, the use of cells of other tissue origin, in particular the human hepatocyte cell line HepG2 and the murine C2C12 myocytes, demonstrated that the abundance of splicing events has been cell type-dependent.
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data from different cell lines shown in Figure 9.

claim: In cDNA samples of Ad5.S-transduced C2C12 cells, only the full-length read-through fragment was detected, indicating no splicing at all.
source: In cDNA samples of Ad5.S-transduced C2C12 cells, only the full-length read-through fragment was detected – indicating no splicing at all (Figure 9C: green arrow).
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: For ChAdOx1-S-transduced C2C12 cells almost exclusively the BGH-pIX splice product was detected.
source: In contrast, for ChAdOx1-S-transduced C2C12 cells almost exclusively the BGH-pIX splice product was detected (Figure 9C: white arrow and Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In ChAdOx1-S-transduced HepG2 cells the Spike-pIX splice product was the predominantly detected fragment.
source: Moreover, in hepatocytes the ratio between full-length and spliced products was again different for Ad5.S- or ChAdOx1-S-transduced cells (Figure 9B). While PCR patterns of Ad5.S-transduced HepG2 cells looked the same as with HeLa cells, in ChAdOx1-S-transduced HepG2 cells the Spike-pIX splice product was the predominantly detected fragment (Figure 9B: blue arrow and Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is based on PCR data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Since Spike-pIX splice products lack the TM-coding sequence, the resulting protein will likely be secreted.
source: Since these splice products lack the TM-coding sequence, the resulting protein will likely be secreted.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of the transmembrane domain.

claim: Out of 9632 reads containing Spike nucleotide sequences in ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells at day 72, a total of 120 trans-spliced mRNAs were identified containing either host cell gene exons fused to Spike sequences or Spike sequences fused to host cell gene exons.
source: In this analysis, we identified, within the 9632 reads containing Spike nucleotide sequences, a total of 120 trans-spliced mRNAs, containing either host cell gene exons (fusing a total of 1 until 18 exons) fused to either the genuine SA of the CMV promoter (n = 8) or the internal Spike SA sites (n = 47). Similarly, we found Spike sequences fused to exons of host cell genes (between 1 and 28 exons). These trans-splicing events occurred either from the Spike open reading frame (n = 32, 32 different SD sites) or from the identified BGH SD sites (n = 33, 1 SD site).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: A total of 50 Spike-pIX fusions were found in the RNA-Seq data from ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells.
source: A total of 50 Spike-pIX fusions were found as well (eight SD sites), while 79 reads were found from the BGH SD to the SA upstream of the pIX-coding sequence as it has been observed with HeLa, HepG2, and C2C12 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: 79 reads were found from the BGH SD to the SA upstream of the pIX-coding sequence in ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells.
source: A total of 50 Spike-pIX fusions were found as well (eight SD sites), while 79 reads were found from the BGH SD to the SA upstream of the pIX-coding sequence as it has been observed with HeLa, HepG2, and C2C12 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The frequency of splicing events was rather low compared to normal Spike reads (1.24–1.33% vs. 97.41%) in ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells.
source: Although the frequency of these splicing event was rather low compared to normal Spike reads (1.24–1.33% vs. 97.41%), their identification was unexpected.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: ABL1 reads were only 44 in the RNA-Seq data from ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells.
source: For comparison, we also determined the number of reads for two housekeeping genes, ABL1 and GAPDH, respectively: ABL1 reads were only 44, while GAPDH reads were 4586.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: GAPDH reads were 4586 in the RNA-Seq data from ChAdOx1-S-transduced MRC-5 cells.
source: For comparison, we also determined the number of reads for two housekeeping genes, ABL1 and GAPDH, respectively: ABL1 reads were only 44, while GAPDH reads were 4586.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The amount of 249 reads that displayed aberrant forms of Spike should be considered as significant compared to housekeeping gene expression.
source: Thus, the amount of 249 reads that displayed aberrant forms of Spike should be considered as significant.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison with housekeeping gene expression levels.

claim: Adenovirus-based vaccines designed to express the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein from a cloned, codon-optimized cDNA may result in unwanted splicing events, if the presence of functional splicing sites in the coding sequence is not avoided during vector design.
source: Here, we provide experimental evidence that adenovirus-based vaccines designed to express the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein from a cloned, codon-optimized cDNA may result in unwanted splicing events, if the presence of functional splicing sites in the coding sequence is not avoided during vector design.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA virus with an infectious cycle that takes place entirely in the cytoplasm.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA virus with an infectious cycle that takes place entirely in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim describes the basic biology of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: There has never been an evolutionary selection against presence of SD and SA sites in SARS-CoV-2 gene sequences.
source: Thus, there has never been an evolutionary selection against presence of SD and SA sites in its gene sequences.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cytoplasmic replication cycle of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: mRNA-based vaccines are functionally only active in the cytoplasm.
source: While mRNA-based vaccines that are functionally only active in the cytoplasm, transcripts from adenoviral vectors are generated in the cell nucleus, where also post-transcriptional RNA processing steps – including splicing – is taking place.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of mRNA vaccines.

claim: Transcripts from adenoviral vectors are generated in the cell nucleus, where post-transcriptional RNA processing steps including splicing take place.
source: While mRNA-based vaccines that are functionally only active in the cytoplasm, transcripts from adenoviral vectors are generated in the cell nucleus, where also post-transcriptional RNA processing steps – including splicing – is taking place.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of adenoviral vector-based vaccines.

claim: Spike protein variants lacking the natural membrane anchor and thereby being subjected to secretion are generated from adenoviral vaccine vectors as a consequence of nuclear RNA splicing events.
source: In this study, we experimentally validated our hypothesis that Spike protein variants lacking the natural membrane anchor – thereby being subjected to secretion – are generated from adenoviral vaccine vectors as a consequence of nuclear RNA splicing events.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: In a Spike/splice reporter system, use of in silico predicted SD sites within the wildtype Spike gene resulted in Spike-Luciferase protein fusion events.
source: We showed (1) that in a Spike/splice reporter system use of in silico predicted SD sites within the wildtype Spike gene resulted in Spike-Luciferase protein fusion events
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the splice reporter system.

claim: In the Spike/splice reporter system, splice reactions lead to secreted protein variants due to the splicing-dependent loss of the TM membrane domain.
source: (2) that in this system splice reactions lead to secreted protein variants due to the splicing-dependent loss of the TM membrane domain
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from the splice reporter system.

claim: Two of the three evaluated adenoviral vectors that encode a Spike gene that is codon-modified for improved expression exhibited more and stronger SD sites than the viral wildtype sequence.
source: (3) that two of the three evaluated adenoviral vectors that encode a Spike gene that is codon-modified for improved expression exhibited more and stronger SD sites than the viral wildtype sequence
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from in silico analysis and experimental validation.

claim: Following transcriptional read-through, splicing occurred to a strong SA in the adenoviral pIX transcript, going along with loss of the TM anchor of Spike.
source: (4) that following transcriptional read-through, splicing occurred to a strong SA in the adenoviral pIX transcript, going also along with loss of the TM anchor of Spike.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from RT-PCR and sequencing experiments.

claim: Soluble Spike protein has been described to cause adverse effects, for example, a strong inflammatory response on endothelial cells.
source: Soluble Spike protein has been described to cause adverse effects, for example, a strong inflammatory response on endothelial cells (Lei et al., 2020; Nuovo et al., 2021; Patra et al., 2020; Amraei and Rahimi, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Severe life-threatening thromboembolic events occur due to infection of recipient cells by wildtype SARS-CoV-2.
source: Obviously, severe life-threatening thromboembolic events occur due to infection of recipient cells by wildtype SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: The claim describes known effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

claim: Pseudoviruses with Spike protein located at their surface may cause strong inflammatory reactions in tissues and endothelial cells, indicating a potential risk of soluble Spike protein to cause severe side effects when systemically present in the vascular system.
source: Even pseudoviruses with Spike protein located at their surface may cause strong inflammatory reactions in tissues and endothelial cells, indicating a potential risk of soluble Spike protein to cause severe side effects when systemically present in the vascular system (Lei et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lei et al., 2021.

claim: Soluble Spike variants could potentially explain the occurrence of rare but severe events observed in particular after vaccination with Vaxzevria.
source: According to our results, soluble Spike variants could potentially explain the occurrence of rare but severe events observed in particular after vaccination with Vaxzevria.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The Ad26.COV2.S vaccine carries fewer SD sequences, especially SD506 and SD3614 are absent.
source: Noteworthy, the Ad26.COV2.S vaccine carries fewer SD sequences, especially SD506 and SD3614 are absent (see Table 2B–D), which are the strongest predicted SD sites in the Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-encoded Spike sequences (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis shown in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: SD506 and SD3614 are the strongest predicted SD sites in the Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-encoded Spike sequences.
source: Noteworthy, the Ad26.COV2.S vaccine carries fewer SD sequences, especially SD506 and SD3614 are absent (see Table 2B–D), which are the strongest predicted SD sites in the Ad5.S- and ChAdOx1-S-encoded Spike sequences (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on in silico analysis shown in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: In contrast to Ad5.S and ChAdOx1-S, no significant amounts of spliced RNA molecules upon cell transduction with Ad26.COV2.S were generated.
source: This was further confirmed by the observation that in contrast to Ad5.S and ChAdOx1-S, no significant amounts of spliced RNA molecules upon cell transduction with Ad26.COV2.S were generated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental RT-PCR data.

claim: The absence of strong SD sites in Ad26.COV2.S may explain the ~3-fold lower incidence for thromboembolic side effects with the Janssen vaccine when compared to the Vaxzevria vaccine.
source: This may explain the ~3-fold lower incidence for thromboembolic side effects with the Janssen vaccine when compared to the Vaxzevria vaccine (see Table 1).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings and clinical data.

claim: The absence of strong SD sites in Ad26.COV2.S may explain the ~2-fold lower risk for TTS with the Janssen vaccine compared to Vaxzevria.
source: It may also explain the ~2-fold lower risk for TTS with the Janssen vaccine.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings and clinical data.

claim: Soluble Spike via its receptor-binding domain will bind to ACE2 and anti-Spike antibodies generated during immunization will recognize Spike variants bound to the endothelial cell surface.
source: Based on our data we pose the hypothesis that soluble Spike via its receptor-binding domain will bind to ACE2 and anti-Spike antibodies generated during immunization will recognize Spike variants, bound to the endothelial cell surface.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Inflammatory reactions could locally occur through different mechanisms including antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), both of which could serve as starting point for thrombus formation.
source: Inflammatory reactions could locally occur through different mechanisms including antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), both of which could serve as starting point for thrombus formation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on known immunological mechanisms.

claim: In ADCC, mainly NK cells are recruited to surface-bound antibodies via Fc-gamma receptors (CD16 or CD32) and cause cell lysis after their activation.
source: In ADCC, mainly NK cells are recruited to surface-bound antibodies via Fc-gamma receptors (CD16 or CD32) and cause cell lysis after their activation.
evidence: The claim describes a known immunological mechanism.

claim: In CDC, anti-Spike antibody-coated endothelial cells may recruit and activate complement that may result in platelet activation via binding of C3 and terminal complement complex on the surface of platelets and thrombin/serotonin secretion.
source: In CDC, anti-Spike antibody-coated endothelial cells may recruit and activate complement that may result in platelet activation via binding of C3 and terminal complement complex on the surface of platelets and thrombin/serotonin secretion (Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2020.

claim: Thromboses may occur in any site of the human body where endothelial cells express ACE2.
source: By this means, thromboses may occur in any site of the human body where endothelial cells express ACE2.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Due to the absence of venous valves, bi-directional and posture-dependent blood flow in the dural venous sinus increases the residence time of soluble Spike protein and enhances the possibility to bind to endothelial cells expressing ACE2.
source: It is conceivable that due to the absence of venous valves bi-directional and posture-dependent blood flow in the dural venous sinus, the residence time of soluble Spike protein is increased and the possibility to bind to endothelial cells expressing ACE2 enhanced.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about why CVST occurs.

claim: Increased residence time of soluble Spike protein in the dural venous sinus could increase the probability of adverse immune reactions at places of slow blood flow.
source: This could increase the probability of adverse immune reactions at places of slow blood flow.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The VITT syndrome has been described as a complex inflammatory process related to HIT, involving the induction of anti-PF4 autoantibodies and platelet activation in a subset of patients.
source: Recently the VITT syndrome has been described, suggesting a complex inflammatory process. Related to HIT it has been reported that the induction of anti-PF4 autoantibodies and platelet activation in a subset of patients may result in the observed combination of thrombocytopenia and thromboses mainly in large vessels including cerebral venous sinus (Figure 11, left side).
evidence: The claim describes a known mechanism of VITT.

claim: Protein impurities from the vaccine production process may be involved in the generation of a pro-inflammatory status.
source: Additionally, it is possible that protein impurities from the vaccine production process may be involved in the generation of a pro-inflammatory status (Krutzke et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krutzke et al., 2021.

claim: ACE2-bound Spike will become a target of anti-Spike antibodies generated after vaccination with the potential to result in ADCC- and/or CDC-mediated inflammatory reactions.
source: These ACE2-bound Spike will then become a target of anti-Spike antibodies, generated after vaccination with the potential to result in ADCC- and/or CDC-mediated inflammatory reactions.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Soluble Spike binding to ACE2 on endothelial cells may cause the NET reaction of neutrophils that has been causally linked to thromboembolic events.
source: It may also cause the already described NET reaction of neutrophils that has been causally linked to thromboembolic events (Schönrich et al., 2020; Veras et al., 2020; Middleton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schönrich et al., 2020; Veras et al., 2020; Middleton et al., 2020.

claim: The rarely observed capillary leak syndrome (Clarkson disease) could potentially be explained by the proposed mechanism of soluble Spike binding to endothelial cells.
source: Also the rarely observed capillary leak syndrome (Clarkson disease; Kawabe et al., 2002) could potentially be explained by such a mechanism.
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citation to Kawabe et al., 2002.

claim: Strong SD sites should be avoided in DNA-encoded sequences, especially when derived from RNA viruses.
source: Taken together, from our work it appears that for DNA-encoded sequences (especially when derived from RNA viruses), most importantly, strong SDs should be avoided and strong poly(A) signals should be used for RNA termination in expression constructs.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Strong poly(A) signals should be used for RNA termination in expression constructs for DNA-encoded sequences.
source: Taken together, from our work it appears that for DNA-encoded sequences (especially when derived from RNA viruses), most importantly, strong SDs should be avoided and strong poly(A) signals should be used for RNA termination in expression constructs.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Transgene sequences in adenoviral vectors are usually embedded in the adenoviral genome in the gap of the deleted E1-region, located directly upstream of the adenoviral pIX with a strong SA site.
source: Usually, transgenes sequences are embedded in the adenoviral genome in the gap of the deleted E1-region, located directly upstream of the adenoviral pIX with a strong SA site.
evidence: The claim describes the typical design of adenoviral vectors.

claim: An inversion of the expression cassette in adenoviral vectors would avoid splicing events to occur between the transgenic-coding sequence and the viral pIX transcript.
source: Alternatively, while most transgenes in adenoviral vectors have a 'left-to-right' orientation, also an inversion of the expression cassette would avoid splicing events to occur between the transgenic-coding sequence and the viral pIX transcript.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future vector design.

claim: Following intramuscular injection of adenovirus vectors in mice, significant amounts of adenovirus vectors end up in hepatocytes, where expression of the transgene occurs.
source: In mice, it has been observed that following intramuscular injection significant amounts of adenovirus vectors end up in hepatocytes, where expression of the transgene occurs (Kron et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kron et al., 2011.

claim: It is likely that the chimpanzee ChAdOx1-S is also a hepatotropic adenovirus, since it is based on the chimpanzee adenovirus Y25, which belonged to a group of isolates from chimpanzees associated with outbreaks of viral hepatitis.
source: It is likely that the chimpanzee ChAdOx1-S is also a hepatotropic adenovirus, since it is based on the chimpanzee adenovirus Y25 (Dicks et al., 2012), which belonged to a group of isolates from chimpanzees associated with outbreaks of viral hepatitis (Hillis and Goodman, 1969).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to Dicks et al., 2012 and Hillis and Goodman, 1969.

claim: If transduction of hepatocytes would occur in vaccines after intramuscular injection in a significant amount, larger amounts of Spike proteins having lost the transmembrane domain by splicing will be secreted into the systemic circulation via the hepatic veins.
source: If transduction of hepatocytes would occur in (some of the) vaccines after intramuscular injection in a significant amount, it is conceivable that larger amounts of Spike proteins, having lost the transmembrane domain by splicing, will be secreted into the systemic circulation via the hepatic veins.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings and known biology.
